cases.reasoning: Both replies use the request's files and constraints correctly, give a parse/serialize plan with a fixed param order, and cover the tests, Suspense and debounce concerns. A puts a dedicated non-goals list, the URL contract table and the scope before the implementation plan, which matches the criterion of stating these before implementation begins. B scatters the non-goals into a recap after the plan. A also decides how top-nav should read the query (window.location at submit time) and explains why, where B hedges between two options. A's Assumptions and Risks sections are mostly substantive, though a few assumptions (for example that the clear buttons exist) are hedged. B is slightly tighter and adds a useful manual check with npx serve, but it is less decisive overall.

The request gives no stack, so neither reply can name real files. Both handle this honestly with bracketed placeholders and clear scope. A prefills sensible defaults (follow the OS setting, header toggle) so the brief is usable as-is. It also states explicit in/out scope and asks three focused questions at the end. B is more compact and offers a useful tip to split the work into two tasks, but it leaves many more brackets to fill and asks for a theme-logic test that adds work to a task the user wanted quick. A's Risks and Next actions sections are somewhat padded, which narrows the gap. On balance A's stated assumptions, hydration note and stronger non-goals make it a little more useful.

Both replies push back on the same three risky requests: Codex running the production migration, merging and deploying, and skipping tests. Both keep the work to a PR, additive migrations, and a minimal four-case test set. A's acceptance criteria are more checkable. They include that PAYMENT_PROVIDER=stripe still works as a rollback, that the migration SQL is in the PR, and a list of what the PR description must contain. A also has a concrete env-var switch, --create-only for the migration, and a clear assumptions list with two focused questions (subscriptions, live keys). B is good and adds useful details (the cancel endpoint, webhook URL registration, merchant review for live keys), but its completion criteria are thinner and its rollback is vaguer (a feature flag). A invents a Mon-Wed schedule, a minor flaw. Overall A is slightly stronger.
